steps.body: A **function** is a rule that takes an input and gives back exactly ONE output — like a machine: put a number in, get exactly one number out. A drink machine where pressing 'cola' always dispenses cola is a function; pressing one button and getting a random drink is not.
Feed the machine an input and watch its rule produce exactly one output. Change the input and the output follows — that single, predictable output is what makes it a function.

widget.prompt: Find the input that makes this machine output 10.
widget.successFeedback: Input 4 → 3 × 4 − 2 = 10. Each input gives exactly one output — that's the rule of a function.
widget.lowFeedback: The output is below 10 — the rule needs a larger input to get there.
widget.highFeedback: The output is above 10 — try a smaller input.

predict.prompt: To find the INPUT that makes the machine output 10, will you undo its steps in FORWARD order or BACKWARD order?

options.label: Backward — undo the last step first
Forward — same order as the machine
Either order works

predict.reveal: Unwrapping reverses wrapping: the machine's LAST move gets undone FIRST — from 10, add back the 2 to get 12, then divide by 3 to reach input 4. Forward order fails here: 10 ÷ 3 ≈ 3.3, plus 2 gives about 5.3, and 5.3 fed into the machine doesn't return 10. Working backward through the steps walks the output home to its input.

cml.actionGoal: Vary the input and coordinate the output, table row, graph point, and equation.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Increase the input by one repeatedly. What pattern must appear in the outputs, table, and graph?

explanation.prompt: What makes this mapping a function?

options.label: Each input is transformed by the same rule into exactly one output.
options.feedback: Exactly. A function requires one output per input, not unique outputs overall.

options.label: Different inputs must always have different outputs.
options.feedback: That describes a surface feature, not the mathematical relationship that must remain true. A function requires one output per input, not unique outputs overall.

widget.prompt: Which of these acts like a function?

options.label: A vending machine where button B3 always gives the same snack
options.feedback: Right — one input (B3) always maps to exactly one output (that snack).

options.label: A machine where button B3 gives a random snack each time
options.feedback: That's NOT a function — the same input (B3) can give different outputs, breaking the one-output rule.

options.label: A machine with no buttons at all
options.feedback: Without inputs there's nothing to map — a function needs inputs that each produce one output.

options.label: A machine where pressing any button breaks it
options.feedback: That produces no reliable output at all — a function must give exactly one output per input.

steps.body: The key test: for each input, is there exactly ONE output? If a single input could give two different outputs, it's not a function. If different inputs happen to share the same output, that's totally fine — that rule can still be a function.

explanationVariants: Each person has exactly one birthday, so 'person → birthday' is a function.
No person can have two different birthdays, so every input maps to one output.

widget.prompt: Is the rule 'each person → their birthday' a function?

options.label: Yes — each person has exactly one birthday
options.feedback: Right — one input (person) always gives one output (birthday).

options.label: No — because many people share the same birthday
options.feedback: Different inputs sharing an output is fine — what matters is that each single person has only ONE birthday, which they do.

options.label: No — birthdays repeat every year
options.feedback: A person's birth DATE is a single fixed value — the rule still gives one output per person.

options.label: Only if everyone has a different birthday
options.feedback: Functions don't require unique outputs — they just require one output per input.

steps.body: See a mapping that breaks the rule.

widget.prompt: Why is 'a student → a class they take' usually NOT a function?

panels.title: Step 1
panels.body: Take one student as the input.

panels.title: Step 2
panels.body: That student takes Math, Science, AND History — three different classes.

panels.title: Step 3
panels.body: One input (the student) gives THREE outputs, so it breaks the one-output rule — not a function.

widget.successFeedback: Exactly — one input producing several outputs is the signature of a non-function.

steps.body: Different inputs, same output — still a function?
explanationVariants: Yes — many students can share one teacher, but each student still has exactly one output, so it's a function.
Repeated outputs across different inputs are allowed; only repeated outputs FROM ONE input break the rule.

widget.prompt: Rule: 'each student → their homeroom teacher.' Thirty students share Mr. Lee. Is it a function?

options.label: Yes — each student has exactly one teacher
options.feedback: Right — sharing an output across inputs is fine; each single student still maps to one teacher.

options.label: No — because thirty students share one teacher
options.feedback: Shared outputs are allowed — the rule only fails if ONE student had two teachers, which isn't the case.

options.label: No — a teacher can't be an output
options.feedback: Anything can be an output — a name, a number, a teacher. What matters is one output per input.

options.label: Only if each student had a different teacher
options.feedback: Functions don't require unique outputs — repeats across inputs are fine.

explanationVariants: 'A number → a number that adds with it to make 10' gives one output (10 minus the input) — a function. The others each let one input map to several outputs.
Only the 'adds to 10' rule assigns exactly one output to each input.

widget.prompt: Which of these is a FUNCTION?

options.label: Each number → the number that adds with it to make 10
options.feedback: Right — every input has exactly one partner (10 minus it).

options.label: Each number → a number smaller than it
options.feedback: One input has MANY smaller numbers — that's several outputs, so not a function.

options.label: Each person → a movie they like
options.feedback: A person can like many movies — several outputs for one input, not a function.

options.label: Each city → a person who lives there
options.feedback: A city has many residents — one input, many outputs, so not a function.

steps.body: Sort rules into functions and non-functions.
explanationVariants: Functions: 'number → its double' and 'person → their age' (one output each). Not functions: 'number → its factors' and 'person → a friend' (many outputs each).
Check each: does every single input give exactly one output? Only then is it a function.

widget.prompt: Sort each rule: function or not?

items.label: each number → its double
items.feedback: Doubling gives exactly one output per input — a function.

items.label: each number → all its factors
items.feedback: A number has many factors — one input, many outputs, so not a function.

items.label: each person → their exact age in years
items.feedback: Each person has exactly one age — a function.

items.label: each person → a friend of theirs
items.feedback: A person can have many friends — one input, many outputs, so not a function.

items.label: each square → its area
items.feedback: A square of a given size has exactly one area — a function.

widget.missFeedback: Not quite — recheck each rule: does every single input give exactly ONE output?
widget.successFeedback: All sorted — a function gives exactly one output per input, no matter how the outputs repeat.

hints: For each rule, pick one input and ask: how many outputs does it produce?
'Double' and 'exact age' give one output each; 'all factors' and 'a friend' give many.
Functions: 'number → its double', 'person → their age', 'square → its area'. Not functions: 'number → its factors', 'person → a friend'.

steps.body: A function gives exactly one output for each input — that's the whole rule.
takeaways: One input → exactly one output means it's a function.
One input → several outputs means it's NOT a function.
Different inputs sharing an output is perfectly fine.

concept.body: A function gives exactly ONE output for each input. If one input could give two different outputs, it's not a function. Different inputs sharing an output is allowed.

explanationVariants: Each number has exactly one square, so 'number → its square' is a function.
Squaring gives one output per input, so it passes the function test.

widget.prompt: Is 'each number → its square' a function?

options.label: Yes — each number has exactly one square
options.feedback: Right — one input gives one output.

options.label: No — because 2 and −2 both square to 4
options.feedback: Different inputs sharing an output is fine — each single number still has one square.

options.label: No — squares get too big
options.feedback: Output size doesn't matter — each input still gives exactly one output.

options.label: Only for positive numbers
options.feedback: Every number, positive or negative, has exactly one square — it's a function throughout.
